zones.description: Learn the fundamental ideas behind data, models, learning and prediction.

checkpoints.subtitle: From rules to systems that learn from data
checkpoints.title: What is Machine Learning?

codeExamples.code:
memory = {"free money now": 1, "meeting at 3pm": 0}  # memorized examples

print(memory.get("free money now"))  # 1: seen during training
print(memory.get("win a prize"))     # None: unseen, memory has no answer

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: a spam filter. Training: it is shown 10,000 emails already marked spam or not spam, and it learns which patterns go with spam. Inference: a new email arrives and the model outputs spam or not spam. A filter that only remembered those 10,000 emails would fail on the next one, and generalization is what separates the two.

quickCheck.explanation: Inference is using a finished model on new data. Training is the earlier step that changes the parameters, and labelling is data preparation, not prediction.
options: Training: the filter updates its parameters
Data labelling: a person marks the email
Inference: the trained model predicts a label for a new input
Feature selection: the model chooses new features
quickCheck.question: A spam filter was trained on 10,000 labelled emails. Which step happens when it classifies an email that arrives tomorrow?

theory.body: Traditional programming: rules + input → program → output. A person writes the rules. Machine learning reverses the direction: examples (data) + a learning algorithm → a model. The rules are learned from the examples instead of being written by hand.
theory.heading: Rules vs learning

theory.body: A model is a learned function. It takes inputs and produces an output, such as a predicted price or a spam probability. Training chooses the numbers inside the function. Nothing about it is magic: it is a formula whose parameters came from data.
theory.heading: What a model is

theory.body: Training: the algorithm adjusts the model using labelled examples. Inference: the finished model receives a new input and produces a prediction. Training happens once or occasionally; inference happens every time the model is used.
theory.heading: Training and inference

theory.body: Memorizing the training examples is not learning. A useful model must work on examples it has never seen. That ability is generalization, and it is the real goal of training.
theory.heading: Generalization

workspace.title: What is Machine Learning?

checkpoints.subtitle: Turn real-world examples into something a model can learn from
checkpoints.title: Data, Features & Labels

codeExamples.code:
# Each row is one house: [area, bedrooms, age, sale price in thousands]
dataset = [
    [1200, 2, 10, 45],
    [1800, 3, 4, 72],
    [900, 1, 15, 32],
]

X = [row[:-1] for row in dataset]  # features: every column except the price
y = [row[-1] for row in dataset]   # labels: the price column

print(X[0], y[0])  # [1200, 2, 10] 45

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: row 1 is a house with area 1200, 2 bedrooms and age 10 that sold for 45 (thousands). Its sample is x = [1200, 2, 10] and its label is y = 45.

quickCheck.explanation: The label is the target the model learns to predict, here the sale price. The other columns are features, the inputs the model receives.
options: Sale Price
Bedrooms
Age
Area
quickCheck.question: A table has the columns Bedrooms, Sale Price, Age and Area. If the model should predict the sale price of a new house, which column is the label y?

theory.body: A dataset is a table of examples, and each row is one sample. For house prices, each row records a house that sold: its Area, Bedrooms, Age and Sale Price. Sale Price is known for past houses, which is why the model can learn from them.
theory.heading: Samples

theory.body: Features are the inputs the model may use: Area, Bedrooms and Age. One house becomes a feature vector x = [area, bedrooms, age], for example [1200, 2, 10].
theory.heading: Features (X)

theory.body: The label is the target the model learns to predict. Here it is Sale Price, so y is the sale price. For a new house the price is unknown, which is exactly why we want the model to estimate it.
theory.heading: Labels (y)

theory.body: All feature rows together form X; all targets together form y. Training uses both. A new house gives a new x, and the trained model estimates its y.
theory.heading: X and y together

workspace.title: Data, Features & Labels

checkpoints.subtitle: Build your first model by minimizing prediction error
checkpoints.title: Linear Regression — The Line That Learns

animation.title: Linear Regression — The Line That Learns

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: hours 1 to 5 with scores 42, 51, 61, 68, 78. The line ŷ = 9x + 33 predicts 42, 51, 60, 69, 78. The residuals are 0, 0, 1, −1 and 0, so MSE = 2 / 5 = 0.4. A flat line at zero would have MSE of about 3758.8.

quickCheck.explanation: The residual is actual − predicted = 61 − 60 = +1. A positive residual means the model under-predicted this student's score.
quickCheck.question: A student studies 3 hours. The model predicts a score of 60, but the actual score is 61. What is the residual, actual minus predicted?

theory.body: Suppose we want to predict an exam score from the hours a student studied. Each student is one sample: x is the hours studied and y is the exam score.
theory.heading: Study hours to exam score

theory.body: A linear model predicts ŷ = w·x + b. The slope w says how many points each extra hour adds, and the intercept b is the predicted score at zero hours. Training means choosing w and b.
theory.heading: A line as the model

theory.body: The residual is actual − predicted. The mean squared error (MSE) averages the squared residuals: MSE = average((predicted − actual)²). Squaring stops positive and negative errors from cancelling, and it makes large misses count more.
theory.heading: Error and MSE

theory.body: Different lines fit the same points very differently. The line with the smaller MSE fits this data better. Training searches for the w and b that make MSE small. How that search works is covered in the Gradient Descent checkpoint.
theory.heading: Better parameters, lower error

workspace.title: Linear Regression — The Line That Learns

checkpoints.subtitle: Why you hold data back, and what each split is for
checkpoints.title: Training, Validation & Testing

codeExamples.code:
import random

def train_val_test_split(rows, val_fraction=0.15, test_fraction=0.15, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    shuffled = rows[:]
    rng.shuffle(shuffled)
    n = len(shuffled)
    n_test = int(n * test_fraction)
    n_val = int(n * val_fraction)
    test = shuffled[:n_test]
    val = shuffled[n_test:n_test + n_val]
    train = shuffled[n_test + n_val:]
    return train, val, test

rows = list(range(100))
train, val, test = train_val_test_split(rows)
print(len(train), len(val), len(test))  # 70 15 15

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: 100 houses split 70 / 15 / 15. Model A has validation error 4.2 and model B has 3.1, so you choose B. If you retrain B on training plus validation data, the test set still gives one honest number, for example 3.5.

quickCheck.explanation: The test set was never used to train or to choose settings, so its score estimates performance on new data. The validation score is biased by repeated tuning, and the training score is biased by fitting.
options: The training set
The test set, used once after all choices are fixed
The validation set, after many rounds of tuning
Whichever set has the highest accuracy
quickCheck.question: Which dataset should be used for the final, unbiased estimate of performance on new data?

theory.body: If the model sees every example while it is being fitted, its score only shows how well it memorized them. To estimate performance on unseen examples, some data has to be held back while the model is built.
theory.heading: Why not train on everything?

theory.body: The training set fits the model's parameters. The validation set compares choices, such as model type or settings, and helps detect overfitting. The test set is used once, at the end, for the final unbiased evaluation.
theory.heading: Three sets, three jobs

theory.body: A common example is 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. This is an illustration, not a required ratio. The right split depends on how much data you have.
theory.heading: An illustrative split

theory.body: If information from validation or test examples influences training, the reported score is too optimistic. For example, computing scaling statistics on all the data leaks the test set into training. Keep held-out examples out of every training decision.
theory.heading: Data leakage

workspace.title: Training, Validation & Testing

checkpoints.subtitle: Why a model that is too simple or too flexible both fail
checkpoints.title: Generalization, Underfitting & Overfitting

codeExamples.code:
def mean_squared_error(predictions, actuals):
    return sum((p - a) ** 2 for p, a in zip(predictions, actuals)) / len(actuals)

actuals = [1, 9, 4]

# A model that predicts the same value everywhere is too simple here.
print(mean_squared_error([5, 5, 5], actuals))   # 11.0  (underfit: high error)

# A model that memorized these exact points is perfect on them.
print(mean_squared_error([1, 9, 4], actuals))   # 0.0   (training error only)

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: points follow a gentle curve. A straight line misses the curve across the whole range (underfit). A degree-10 polynomial passes through every training point but swings wildly between them (overfit). A quadratic follows the curve and does well on new points (balanced).

quickCheck.explanation: A 28-point gap between training and validation accuracy is the overfitting pattern. The model learned the training examples, including their noise, and does not carry that over to unseen examples.
options: The model generalizes well
The validation set is too large
The model is underfitting
The model is overfitting
quickCheck.question: A model has 99% training accuracy and 71% validation accuracy. What is the most likely problem?

theory.body: Training error only tells you how well the model fits examples it has already seen. What we need is performance on new examples. That is generalization.
theory.heading: The goal is unseen data

theory.body: An underfitting model is too simple for the pattern. A flat line through data that follows a curve misses the trend, so the error stays high on training examples and on validation examples too.
theory.heading: Underfitting

theory.body: An overfitting model is flexible enough to follow the noise in the training examples. Its training error becomes very low, but its validation error rises because the noise does not repeat in new data.
theory.heading: Overfitting

theory.body: A good fit captures the main trend without memorizing the noise, so training and validation errors both stay low. The goal is not the lowest training error. The goal is performance on unseen data.
theory.heading: A good fit and the real goal

workspace.title: Generalization, Underfitting & Overfitting

checkpoints.subtitle: Learning from known answers versus discovering structure
checkpoints.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning

codeExamples.code:
emails = [
    {"words": 3, "label": "spam"},
    {"words": 40, "label": "not spam"},
]

# Supervised: the learner receives (x, y) pairs.
supervised_examples = [(e["words"], e["label"]) for e in emails]

# Unsupervised: the learner receives only x.
unsupervised_inputs = [e["words"] for e in emails]

print(supervised_examples)  # [(3, 'spam'), (40, 'not spam')]
print(unsupervised_inputs)  # [3, 40]

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: a list of emails with a word count and a label. Supervised learning receives pairs (word count, label). Unsupervised learning receives only the word counts and must find patterns without being told which emails are spam.

quickCheck.explanation: The shopper segments are not given in the data, so the algorithm must discover them from the features. The loan and house-price examples both have known answers to learn from, so they are supervised.
options: Predict whether a loan will default, using past loans labelled as defaulted or repaid
Estimate a house price from past sales that have known prices
Group shoppers into segments using purchase histories that have no segment labels
quickCheck.question: Which scenario is unsupervised learning?

theory.body: Every training example has a target y. The model learns a mapping from X to y. Classification predicts a category, such as spam or not spam. Regression predicts a number, such as a house price.
theory.heading: Supervised: learn from known answers

theory.body: Only the inputs X are given. The algorithm looks for structure, such as clusters of similar examples (clustering), or a smaller set of features that still describes the data well (dimensionality reduction).
theory.heading: Unsupervised: find structure in X

theory.body: Ask: do I already know the answer I want the model to learn from? If yes, the problem is usually supervised. If not, and the goal is to discover groups or structure, it is usually unsupervised.
theory.heading: How to decide

theory.body: Emails labelled spam or not spam support supervised classification. The same emails without labels, grouped by their wording, support unsupervised clustering.
theory.heading: Same data, different question

workspace.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning

checkpoints.subtitle: From a vague goal to a model you can trust
checkpoints.title: The Machine Learning Workflow

codeExamples.code:
def split(data):
    n = len(data)
    return data[:int(0.7 * n)], data[int(0.7 * n):int(0.85 * n)], data[int(0.85 * n):]

def run_workflow(data, train_fn, eval_fn):
    train, val, test = split(data)     # split the data
    model = train_fn(train)            # train on the training set
    val_score = eval_fn(model, val)    # evaluate on validation
    return model, val_score            # test is reserved for the final report

houses = list(range(20))
model, score = run_workflow(
    houses,
    lambda t: sum(t) / len(t),
    lambda m, v: sum(abs(m - x) for x in v) / len(v),
)
print(round(model, 2), round(score, 2))  # 6.5 8.5

workspace.learnMore: Worked example, one house-price model throughout. Goal: predict sale price. Features: area, bedrooms, age. Target: sale price. Split 1,000 past sales into 70 / 15 / 15. Train a simple regression on the training houses. Validation error is too high, so you add a feature and retrain. Measure the test houses once and report that error. A new house then gets an estimated price.

quickCheck.explanation: Validation results guide improvements. Only after the model and its settings are fixed should the test houses be measured, once, for the final estimate. Adjusting the model after seeing test results makes that estimate optimistic.
options: Retrain the model on the test houses to improve it
Finish improving the model using validation results, so every choice is fixed
Check the test error repeatedly and adjust the features each time
Remove the validation houses to save space
quickCheck.question: You have trained a house-price model and are improving it by checking errors on the validation houses. What should happen before you measure the test houses?

theory.body: Define the problem, collect and understand the data, choose the features and the target, and split the data. Then choose a simple model and train it on the training houses only.
theory.heading: From goal to model

theory.body: Measure the error on validation houses. If it is too high, improve the features or the model and validate again. Only after every choice is fixed should the test houses be measured, and that happens once.
theory.heading: Validate, improve, test once

theory.body: Inference: give the model a new house's features and it returns an estimated price. The model estimates the price; it does not look it up.
theory.heading: Use the model

theory.body: Real markets change over time: prices move and neighbourhoods change. Keep watching the errors after release, and revisit the model when they drift.
theory.heading: Monitor

checkpoints.subtitle: How a table of houses becomes numbers a computer can work with
checkpoints.title: Vectors & Matrices

codeExamples.code:
X = [
    [1200, 2, 10],
    [1800, 3, 4],
    [900, 1, 15],
]

print(len(X), len(X[0]))              # 3 3  (rows, columns)
areas = [row[0] for row in X]         # column 1: every area
Xt = [list(col) for col in zip(*X)]   # the transpose
print(areas)                          # [1200, 1800, 900]
print(Xt[0])                          # [1200, 1800, 900]

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: X = [[1200, 2, 10], [1800, 3, 4], [900, 1, 15]]. Row 2 is the house [1800, 3, 4]. Column 1 is every area: [1200, 1800, 900]. The first row of Xᵀ is that same list of areas.

quickCheck.explanation: Each house is one row and each feature is one column, so 500 houses with 4 features give 500 rows and 4 columns.
quickCheck.question: A dataset has 500 houses, each described by 4 features. What shape is its feature matrix X (rows × columns)?

theory.body: A scalar is a single number, such as the area of one house: 1200. One feature of one example is a scalar.
theory.heading: A scalar is one number

theory.body: Write one house's features in a fixed order and you get a vector: x = [1200, 2, 10] for area, bedrooms and age. The number of entries is the vector's dimension, so x is 3-dimensional. The order matters: the first entry is always the area.
theory.heading: A vector is an ordered list

theory.body: Stack one vector per house, one on each row, and you get a matrix X. With 3 houses and 3 features, X has 3 rows and 3 columns. Row i is house i, and column j is feature j.
theory.heading: A matrix is a table of vectors

theory.body: The transpose Xᵀ flips the table so rows become columns. The first column of X (every house's area) becomes the first row of Xᵀ. In machine learning, a dataset is exactly this: a matrix with one row per example and one column per feature.
theory.heading: The transpose swaps rows and columns

workspace.title: Vectors & Matrices

checkpoints.subtitle: Everything you can reach by scaling and adding vectors
checkpoints.title: Vector Spaces and Subspaces

codeExamples.code:
def combine(a, v, b, w):
    return [a * x + b * y for x, y in zip(v, w)]

print(combine(3, [1, 0], 4, [0, 1]))   # [3, 4]

# The span of v = [1, 2] is the line y = 2x.
def on_line(p):
    return p[1] == 2 * p[0]

print(on_line([2, 4]), on_line([2, 5]))  # True False

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: with v = [1, 0] and w = [0, 1], any point [a, b] is a·v + b·w, so [3, 4] = 3v + 4w. With only v = [1, 2], you can reach [2, 4] (it is 2v) but not [2, 5]: the span of v is the line y = 2x.

quickCheck.explanation: If one vector is a multiple of the other, combining them only ever moves along that one line. To reach the whole plane you need two vectors that point in genuinely different directions.
options: The whole plane
A single point
A circle around the origin
A line through the origin
quickCheck.question: Two vectors in the plane point along the same line (one is a multiple of the other). What do all of their linear combinations form?

theory.body: Two things can be done to vectors: scale them (multiply by a number) and add them. A linear combination uses both: a·v + b·w. For v = [2, 1] and w = [−1, 2], taking a = 1.5 and b = 1 gives [2, 3.5].
theory.heading: Scale and add

theory.body: The span of some vectors is the set of all their linear combinations. One vector spans a line through the origin. Two vectors that do not point along the same line span the whole plane.
theory.heading: The span is everything you can reach

theory.body: A subspace is a line, plane or higher-dimensional flat space that contains the origin and never lets you escape: adding two vectors in it, or scaling one, stays inside it. A line through the origin is a subspace of the plane. A line that misses the origin is not.
theory.heading: A subspace is a flat space through the origin

theory.body: Real data often lies close to a line or plane inside a much bigger feature space. If you can find that subspace, you can describe each example with fewer numbers, which is the idea behind dimensionality reduction.
theory.heading: Why it matters for ML

workspace.title: Vector Spaces and Subspaces

checkpoints.subtitle: The dot product, and what it means for two vectors to be perpendicular
checkpoints.title: Orthogonality

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: u = [3, 0] and v = [0, 2.5] give 3·0 + 0·2.5 = 0, so they are orthogonal. Rotate v to [2.5, 0] and the dot product becomes 7.5, the largest value possible for these two lengths.

quickCheck.explanation: A zero dot product between non-zero vectors means they are orthogonal (perpendicular). It says nothing about their lengths, and neither vector needs to be zero.
options: They are perpendicular
They point in the same direction
They have the same length
One of them must be the zero vector
quickCheck.question: u and v are two non-zero vectors with u · v = 0. What does that tell you?

theory.body: Multiply matching entries of two vectors and add: u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂. The result is a single number that says how much the two vectors point the same way. For u = [1, 2] and v = [3, 1], u · v = 3 + 2 = 5.
theory.heading: The dot product measures agreement

theory.body: A positive dot product means the vectors point in broadly the same direction. A negative one means they point in broadly opposite directions. A dot product of exactly zero means they are perpendicular.
theory.heading: Positive, negative, zero

theory.body: Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal when u · v = 0. For u = [1, 0] and v = [0, 1] it is 1·0 + 0·1 = 0. Also [1, 2] · [2, −1] = 2 − 2 = 0. Orthogonal is the mathematical word for perpendicular.
theory.heading: Orthogonal means dot product 0

theory.body: Orthogonal directions carry independent information: moving along one does not change your position along the other. That makes coordinates easy to read off, and it is what projections, least squares and PCA rely on.
theory.heading: Why ML uses it

workspace.title: Orthogonality

checkpoints.subtitle: The shadow of one vector along another direction
checkpoints.title: Projections

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: a = [4, 3] and b = [5, 2]. a · b = 26 and b · b = 29, so the projection is (26/29)·b ≈ [4.48, 1.79]. The residual is about [−0.48, 1.21], and its dot product with b is 0.

quickCheck.explanation: The projection is the best approximation of a using only the direction b: the closest point to a on the line along b. The leftover part, the residual, is perpendicular to b.
options: The vector a rotated until it is perpendicular to b
The sum of a and b
The point on the line along b that is closest to a
The length of b scaled by the length of a
quickCheck.question: What does the projection of a onto b represent?

theory.body: Suppose a vector a is complicated, but you may only move along one direction b. The projection of a onto b is the point on that line closest to a: the part of a that points along b, like its shadow.
theory.heading: Approximate with one direction

theory.body: What is left over, a minus its projection, is the residual. It is perpendicular to b. If it were not, you could slide along b to get closer to a.
theory.heading: The residual is perpendicular

theory.body: The projection is proj = ((a · b) / (b · b)) b. The fraction says how many copies of b you need, and multiplying by b places the point on the line. You do not need to memorize it: it is just the shadow measured with dot products.
theory.heading: The formula comes after the picture

theory.body: Projection is the best approximation using limited directions. Least squares projects data onto the predictions a model can make, and PCA projects data onto its main directions.
theory.heading: The ML connection

workspace.title: Projections

checkpoints.subtitle: The best fit when no line is perfect, as a projection
checkpoints.title: Least Squares

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: the best line for those four points has slope 0.8 and intercept 1.5. Its residuals are −0.3, −0.1, 1.1 and −0.7. They add up to 0, and their dot product with the x-values is also 0: the residual is perpendicular to the inputs.

quickCheck.explanation: Least squares minimizes the total of the squared residuals. It deliberately accepts some error at each point in exchange for the smallest overall squared error.
options: The number of points the line touches
The sum of the squared residuals
The largest single residual
The slope of the line
quickCheck.question: A least-squares line does not pass through every data point. What does it minimize?

theory.body: With real data, no single line usually passes through every point. Instead of demanding a perfect fit, we ask for the best line. For the points (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 4), no straight line hits all four.
theory.heading: No perfect line

theory.body: For a candidate line, the residual of each point is actual minus predicted. Square each residual and add them up to get the total squared error. For y = 0.5x + 2 the residuals are −0.5, 0, 1.5, 0 and the total is 2.5.
theory.heading: Residuals and squared errors

theory.body: Try other lines and compare. y = x + 1 gives a total of 2.0, and y = 0.8x + 1.5 gives 1.8. Least squares picks the line with the smallest total squared error: here, y = 0.8x + 1.5.
theory.heading: The best line has the smallest total

theory.body: Write the model's predictions as A x, where the columns of A hold the inputs (and a column of ones) and x holds the slope and intercept. The vector of data values b cannot be matched exactly by any prediction A x. Least squares picks the prediction closest to b: the projection of b onto the space of possible predictions. The leftover error is perpendicular to that space, which leads to the normal equations AᵀA x = Aᵀb. This is how linear regression is fitted.
theory.heading: Why this is a projection

workspace.title: Least Squares

checkpoints.subtitle: The directions a matrix only stretches, never turns
checkpoints.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

codeExamples.code:
A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]

def apply(A, v):
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]

print(apply(A, [1, 0]))    # [2, 1]   direction changed
print(apply(A, [1, 1]))    # [3, 3]   = 3 * [1, 1]
print(apply(A, [1, -1]))   # [1, -1]  = 1 * [1, -1]

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. A·[1, 0] = [2, 1], which points in a different direction. But A·[1, 1] = [3, 3] = 3·[1, 1] and A·[1, −1] = [1, −1] = 1·[1, −1]. So [1, 1] is an eigenvector with λ = 3, and [1, −1] is an eigenvector with λ = 1.

quickCheck.explanation: A v = λ v means the result lies on the same line as v: only its length (and possibly its sign) changes. Other vectors get turned to a new direction.
options: It becomes the zero vector
It is rotated by exactly 90 degrees
It is always shortened
It stays on the same line through the origin, scaled by its eigenvalue
quickCheck.question: What is special about an eigenvector v after it is transformed by A?

theory.body: Multiplying by a matrix A transforms vectors: it can rotate, stretch and shear them. For most vectors, both the direction and the length change.
theory.heading: A matrix moves vectors

theory.body: But for special vectors the result lies on the same line as the original. Such a vector v is an eigenvector of A: A v = λ v. It is only scaled, never turned.
theory.heading: A few directions stay put

theory.body: The number λ is the eigenvalue. λ = 3 means three times as long, λ = 1 means unchanged, a value between 0 and 1 means shrunk, and a negative λ means flipped to the opposite direction.
theory.heading: The eigenvalue is the scale factor

theory.body: The covariance matrix of a dataset describes how the data spreads. Its eigenvectors point along the main directions of spread, and its eigenvalues say how much spread there is along each. PCA is built on exactly this.
theory.heading: Why ML cares

workspace.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

checkpoints.subtitle: Make a hard transformation simple by changing coordinates
checkpoints.title: Matrix Diagonalization

codeExamples.code:
A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]
e1, e2 = [1, 1], [1, -1]     # eigenvectors
d1, d2 = 3, 1                # their eigenvalues

def dot(u, v):
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))

v = [2, 0]
c1, c2 = dot(v, e1) / 2, dot(v, e2) / 2         # 1. change coordinates
s1, s2 = d1 * c1, d2 * c2                       # 2. scale each coordinate
back = [s1 * e1[i] + s2 * e2[i] for i in range(2)]   # 3. change back
direct = [A[0][0] * v[0] + A[0][1] * v[1], A[1][0] * v[0] + A[1][1] * v[1]]
print(back, direct)          # [4.0, 2.0] [4, 2]

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has eigenvectors [1, 1] and [1, −1] with eigenvalues 3 and 1. To apply A to v = [2, 0]: write v = 1·[1, 1] + 1·[1, −1], scale to 3·[1, 1] + 1·[1, −1], and rebuild: [4, 2]. That matches A·v = [4, 2] computed directly.

quickCheck.explanation: D holds the eigenvalues on its diagonal. In the eigenvector coordinates, A simply stretches each axis by its own eigenvalue, with no mixing between axes.
options: How much each eigenvector direction is stretched, independently of the others
The data you want to predict
A rotation that does not change lengths
The inverse of A
quickCheck.question: In A = P D P⁻¹, what does the diagonal matrix D describe?

theory.body: A transformation can look complicated in the usual x-y coordinates but become simple in coordinates built from its eigenvectors, because there it just stretches each axis by a separate amount.
theory.heading: The right coordinates make it simple

theory.body: To apply A to a vector: (1) change coordinates to the eigenvector directions, (2) scale each coordinate by its eigenvalue, (3) change back. As one formula: A = P D P⁻¹.
theory.heading: Three moves

theory.body: D is a diagonal matrix: its only non-zero entries are the eigenvalues on the diagonal. Diagonal means each axis is scaled independently, with no mixing. P holds the eigenvectors as its columns, and P⁻¹ changes coordinates into that basis.
theory.heading: What D means

theory.body: Because D is so simple, repeating A many times just scales each axis many times. It also explains the long-run behaviour of a transformation and underlies PCA. Not every matrix can be diagonalized, but the symmetric ones that appear in ML, like covariance matrices, always can.
theory.heading: Why it is useful

checkpoints.subtitle: Rotate, stretch, rotate: the shape of every matrix
checkpoints.title: Singular Value Decomposition

codeExamples.code:
import math

# For a symmetric matrix [[a, b], [b, d]] with positive eigenvalues,
# the singular values equal the eigenvalues.
a, b, d = 2, 1, 2
gap = math.sqrt((a - d) ** 2 + 4 * b * b)
sigma = [((a + d) + gap) / 2, ((a + d) - gap) / 2]
print(sigma)                                   # [3.0, 1.0]

u = [2 ** -0.5, 2 ** -0.5]                     # direction of the largest stretch
rank1 = [[sigma[0] * p * q for q in u] for p in u]
print([[round(x, 2) for x in row] for row in rank1])   # [[1.5, 1.5], [1.5, 1.5]]
print(sigma[0] ** 2 / sum(s ** 2 for s in sigma))      # 0.9

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: σ₁ = 3 and σ₂ = 1 give 3² / (3² + 1²) = 9/10, so the rank-1 approximation keeps 90% of the matrix's squared size (its 'energy'). Dropping σ₂ throws away the remaining 10%.

quickCheck.explanation: Singular values are the stretch amounts. A large one means the matrix magnifies that direction strongly, so it carries a lot of the matrix's effect. Small singular values are the ones safe to drop.
options: That direction carries almost no information
The data in that direction is just noise
The transformation stretches strongly along that direction, so it matters more
The matrix cannot be transformed
quickCheck.question: What does a large singular value indicate?

theory.body: Any matrix A can be written A = U Σ Vᵀ. Read right to left: Vᵀ rotates the input, Σ stretches along the axes, and U rotates the result. A circle of vectors becomes an ellipse.
theory.heading: Every matrix is rotate, stretch, rotate

theory.body: The stretch amounts on the diagonal of Σ are the singular values, σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ …. A large singular value means that direction matters a lot; a tiny one means it barely matters.
theory.heading: Singular values rank the directions

theory.body: Keep only the largest singular values and set the rest to zero. This rank-k approximation is the best possible matrix of that simplicity. For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], whose singular values are 3 and 1, keeping only σ₁ gives [[1.5, 1.5], [1.5, 1.5]].
theory.heading: Low-rank approximation

theory.body: A smaller, cleaner version of the data supports compression, denoising and dimensionality reduction. PCA, covered later in the course, is closely tied to SVD.
theory.heading: Why ML uses it

checkpoints.subtitle: Matrices that curve upward in every direction
checkpoints.title: Positive Definite Matrices

codeExamples.code:
def quad_form(A, x):
    return sum(x[i] * A[i][j] * x[j] for i in range(len(x)) for j in range(len(x)))

A = [[2, 0], [0, 1]]
B = [[1, 0], [0, -1]]
print(quad_form(A, [1, 1]))                      # 3
print(quad_form(A, [1, 0]), quad_form(A, [0, 1]))   # 2 1   (both positive)
print(quad_form(B, [1, 0]), quad_form(B, [0, 1]))   # 1 -1  (one negative: a saddle)

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: for B = [[1, 0], [0, −1]], x = [1, 0] gives 1 but x = [0, 1] gives −1. One negative value is enough to rule out positive definiteness.

quickCheck.explanation: Positive definite needs every eigenvalue to be positive. A negative eigenvalue means some direction curves downward, so the matrix is not positive definite.
options: Yes, because one eigenvalue is positive
No, because one eigenvalue is negative
Yes, because the eigenvalues add up to a positive number
Only if the matrix is also diagonal
quickCheck.question: A symmetric matrix has eigenvalues 3 and −1. Is it positive definite?

theory.body: For a matrix A and a vector x, the number xᵀ A x is called a quadratic form. For A = [[2, 0], [0, 1]] it equals 2x₁² + x₂². At x = [1, 1] it is 3.
theory.heading: The quadratic form

theory.body: A symmetric matrix A is positive definite if xᵀ A x > 0 for every non-zero x. Imagine the value as a height: positive everywhere means the surface curves up in every direction, like a bowl with one lowest point.
theory.heading: Positive in every direction

theory.body: For a symmetric matrix, being positive definite is the same as having all eigenvalues positive. A = [[2, 0], [0, 1]] has eigenvalues 2 and 1, so it is positive definite. B = [[1, 0], [0, −1]] has eigenvalues 1 and −1, so it is not: xᵀ B x = x₁² − x₂² is negative along the second axis, which gives a saddle.
theory.heading: Eigenvalues give a quick test

theory.body: Covariance matrices are positive (semi-)definite. In optimization, positive curvature in every direction means a stable minimum, so gradient descent settles there. A saddle is a place where it can get stuck.
theory.heading: Why ML cares

checkpoints.subtitle: Why a small nudge to a model should cause only a small change in its error
checkpoints.title: Functions and Continuity

codeExamples.code:
def loss(w):
    return (w - 3) ** 2

def step_rule(w):
    # Not continuous: the output jumps from 0 to 1 at w = 2.
    return 0 if w < 2 else 1

print(round(loss(2.00), 4), round(loss(2.01), 4))   # 1.0 0.9801
print(step_rule(1.999), step_rule(2.0))             # 0 1

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: with L(w) = (w − 3)², L(2.00) = 1 and L(2.01) = 0.9801, a change of only 0.0199. Now count how many of 100 emails a spam filter gets right as a threshold w moves: the count can stay at 91 and then suddenly become 92. That count is step-like, while the loss that measures how far each prediction is from its label moves smoothly.

quickCheck.explanation: Following a slope only works when small changes in the input give small, predictable changes in the output. A jump breaks that, which is why training uses a smooth loss instead.
options: The weight was too large to begin with
Accuracy can only be measured on training data
A tiny nudge causes a sudden jump, so the nearby change gives no smooth direction to follow
Accuracy is always a smooth curve, so this cannot happen
quickCheck.question: A model's accuracy jumps from 80% to 85% when one weight changes by 0.0001. Why is that unhelpful for following the error downhill?

theory.body: A function takes an input and gives back exactly one output. In machine learning the most important function is the loss: you give it a setting of the model, such as a weight w, and it returns one number saying how wrong the model is. Take L(w) = (w − 3)². Put in w = 2 and you get 1. Put in w = 3 and you get 0, a perfect fit.
theory.heading: A function is a rule: input in, output out

theory.body: Draw w along the bottom and the loss as the height. The result is a smooth bowl whose lowest point sits at w = 3. Learning will mean sliding toward the bottom of a picture like this, so it helps to see the shape first.
theory.heading: Plot it to see its shape

theory.body: A function is continuous when you can draw it without lifting your pen: a tiny change in the input causes only a tiny change in the output. For L(w) = (w − 3)², moving w from 2.00 to 2.01 changes the loss from 1 to about 0.98. Compare a rule that outputs 0 for w below 2 and 1 for w at or above 2. At w = 2 the output jumps by a whole 1 although w barely moved, so that rule is not continuous.
theory.heading: Continuous means no jumps

theory.body: If the loss could jump, a tiny tweak might change the error wildly, and standing at one point would tell you nothing about which way to go. A smooth, continuous loss lets us feel our way downhill using only what is nearby. That is why models are trained on a smooth loss, even when the thing we finally care about, such as the count of correct predictions, changes in jumps.
theory.heading: Why learning needs it

workspace.title: Functions and Continuity

checkpoints.subtitle: The slope of a curve at one point, and what it tells a model to do
checkpoints.title: Derivatives

codeExamples.code:
def loss(w):
    return (w - 3) ** 2

def secant_slope(f, w, gap):
    # A numeric estimate: look at two nearby points and divide.
    return (f(w + gap) - f(w)) / gap

for gap in [1.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.001]:
    print(gap, round(secant_slope(loss, 1.0, gap), 3))
# 1.0 -3.0
# 0.5 -3.5
# 0.1 -3.9
# 0.001 -3.999

def exact_slope(w):
    return 2 * (w - 3)     # worked out by hand with the power rule

print(exact_slope(1.0))    # -4.0

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: at w = 5 the derivative of L(w) = (w − 3)² is 2(5 − 3) = +4, so the loss goes up if w increases and down if w decreases. At w = 3 it is 0, the flat bottom. The code below estimates the slope numerically by nudging w, then compares with the exact formula 2(w − 3).

quickCheck.explanation: A positive derivative means the loss rises as the weight rises, so moving the weight down lowers the loss. A derivative of exactly 0 would be the flat spot.
options: Decrease it slightly
Increase it slightly
Leave it, because the loss is already at its minimum
Set it equal to 6
quickCheck.question: At the current weight the derivative of the loss is +6. What should you do to the weight to lower the loss?

theory.body: Take the loss L(w) = (w − 3)² and pick two points on its curve: w = 1 where L = 4, and w = 2 where L = 1. Draw a straight line through them (a secant). Its slope is the change in output divided by the change in input: (1 − 4) / (2 − 1) = −3. On average the loss falls by 3 for every 1 step of w.
theory.heading: Slope between two points

theory.body: Keep the first point at w = 1 and move the second one closer: a gap of 0.5 gives a slope of −3.5, a gap of 0.1 gives −3.9, a gap of 0.001 gives −3.999. The numbers settle toward one value, −4. That value is the steepness of the curve exactly at w = 1.
theory.heading: Slide the second point closer

theory.body: The derivative of L at w, written dL/dw, is the slope the secants settle toward as the gap shrinks to zero. It is also the slope of the tangent line, the straight line that just touches the curve at that point. For L(w) = (w − 3)² the power rule gives dL/dw = 2(w − 3), so at w = 1 it is −4, matching the numbers above.
theory.heading: The derivative is that settled slope

theory.body: If the derivative is negative, raising w lowers the loss. If it is positive, raising w raises the loss. If it is zero, the curve is flat there, as at the bottom of the bowl (w = 3). The size says how sensitive the loss is: a derivative of −4 means a small step in w changes the loss four times as much.
theory.heading: Sign and size

theory.body: The derivative answers two practical questions at once: which way should this weight move to reduce the loss, and how much does the loss react to it? Every training step starts from that answer.
theory.heading: Why a model cares

workspace.title: Derivatives

checkpoints.subtitle: Zooming in until a curve looks like a straight line
checkpoints.title: Linear Approximation

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: L(w) = (w − 3)² at a = 1 has L = 4 and slope −4. Step h = 0.1: predicted 3.6, true 3.61, error 0.01. Step h = 1: predicted 0, true 1, error 1. The step was ten times bigger and the error one hundred times bigger.

quickCheck.explanation: The error equals the step squared, so a step ten times bigger gives an error one hundred times bigger: 0.01 becomes 1. That is why straight-line predictions are trusted only for small steps.
options: Still about 0.01, because the slope is the same
About 0.1, because the step is ten times bigger
About 0.5
About 1, because the error grows much faster than the step
quickCheck.question: A tangent-line prediction for a step of 0.1 is off by 0.01 on L(w) = (w − 3)². About how far off is it for a step of 1.0?

theory.body: Zoom far enough into any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line. The loss L(w) = (w − 3)² is a bowl, but in a tiny window around w = 1 it is almost indistinguishable from its tangent line. That line is easy to work with, so we use it as a stand-in for the curve nearby.
theory.heading: Curves look straight up close

theory.body: Start at a point a. The new value is roughly the old value plus the slope times the step: L(a + h) ≈ L(a) + L'(a) × h. Here a = 1, L(1) = 4 and the slope is −4, so L(1 + h) ≈ 4 − 4h.
theory.heading: The tangent-line recipe

theory.body: For a step h = 0.1 the recipe predicts 4 − 0.4 = 3.6, and the true loss L(1.1) is 3.61. For h = 0.5 it predicts 2.0 while the truth is 2.25. The prediction is close, but never exact, because the curve bends away from the line.
theory.heading: Try it on nearby points

theory.body: For this loss the gap between truth and prediction is exactly h × h: 0.01, 0.25, 1 and 4 for steps 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2. Doubling the step makes the error four times bigger. At h = 2 the line predicts −4, which is impossible for a squared loss. The straight-line picture is only trustworthy for small steps.
theory.heading: The error grows with distance

theory.body: If you know the current loss and slope, you can predict what a small change to a weight will do without recomputing anything: new loss ≈ old loss + slope × change. This is exactly why training takes small steps. Big steps leave the region where the straight-line prediction holds.
theory.heading: Why a model cares

checkpoints.subtitle: How the loss reacts to one knob when every other knob is held still
checkpoints.title: Partial Derivatives

codeExamples.code:
def L(w1, w2):
    return (w1 - 3) ** 2 + 2 * (w2 - 1) ** 2

def dL_dw1(w1, w2):
    return 2 * (w1 - 3)       # w2 is treated as a constant

def dL_dw2(w1, w2):
    return 4 * (w2 - 1)       # w1 is treated as a constant

print(dL_dw1(1, 3), dL_dw2(1, 3))   # -4 8

# A numeric check: nudge ONE weight, hold the other still.
nudge = 0.001
est1 = (L(1 + nudge, 3) - L(1, 3)) / nudge
est2 = (L(1, 3 + nudge) - L(1, 3)) / nudge
print(round(est1, 3), round(est2, 3))   # -3.999 8.002

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: at (w1, w2) = (1, 3), nudge w1 by 0.001 and the loss moves from 12 to about 11.996, so the estimate is −3.999, close to the exact −4. Nudge w2 by 0.001 instead and the loss moves to about 12.008, an estimate of 8.002, close to the exact +8.

quickCheck.explanation: ∂L/∂w1 = 2(w1 − 3) = 2(5 − 3) = 4. The w2 term is held fixed, so it contributes nothing to the slope in the w1 direction.
options: It depends on the value of w2
quickCheck.question: For L(w1, w2) = (w1 − 3)² + 2(w2 − 1)², what is ∂L/∂w1 when w1 = 5?

theory.body: A model usually has several weights, and the loss depends on all of them at once. Take two weights with L(w1, w2) = (w1 − 3)² + 2(w2 − 1)². At w1 = 1 and w2 = 3 the loss is 4 + 8 = 12. We can no longer ask 'what is the slope?' because the answer depends on which knob we turn.
theory.heading: Real models have many knobs

theory.body: To study w1 alone, freeze w2 at 3 and let only w1 vary. The loss becomes (w1 − 3)² + 8, which is just a one-variable curve we already know how to handle. Then do the same the other way: freeze w1 = 1 and vary w2.
theory.heading: Change one, hold the other

theory.body: The slope along one knob, with the others frozen, is a partial derivative. It is written ∂L/∂w1 (read 'partial L, partial w1'). To compute it, treat every other variable as a fixed number. Here ∂L/∂w1 = 2(w1 − 3), which is −4 at w1 = 1, because the 2(w2 − 1)² part is a constant and its slope in w1 is zero. Likewise ∂L/∂w2 = 4(w2 − 1), which is +8 at w2 = 3.
theory.heading: That slope is a partial derivative

theory.body: ∂L/∂w1 = −4 says raising w1 lowers the loss. ∂L/∂w2 = +8 says raising w2 raises the loss, so w2 should go down. Each knob gets its own answer, and w2 reacts twice as strongly as the size of its number suggests, since 8 is larger than 4 in size.
theory.heading: Reading the two numbers

theory.body: You can estimate a partial derivative numerically: nudge one weight by a tiny amount, leave the other alone, and divide the change in loss by the nudge. That is a numeric estimate, a check on the formula. It does not replace the formula, and it needs one extra loss evaluation per weight.
theory.heading: Checking by nudging

workspace.title: Partial Derivatives

checkpoints.subtitle: One arrow that says which way is steepest uphill
checkpoints.title: Gradients

codeExamples.code:
import math

def L(w1, w2):
    return (w1 - 3) ** 2 + 2 * (w2 - 1) ** 2

def gradient(w1, w2):
    return [2 * (w1 - 3), 4 * (w2 - 1)]

g = gradient(1, 3)
print(g, [-v for v in g])          # [-4, 8] [4, -8]
print(round(math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in g)), 2))   # 8.94: how steep

def change_after_step(direction, size=0.1):
    length = math.sqrt(direction[0] ** 2 + direction[1] ** 2)
    w1 = 1 + size * direction[0] / length
    w2 = 3 + size * direction[1] / length
    return round(L(w1, w2) - L(1, 3), 2)

print(change_after_step(g))                 # 0.91: along the gradient, loss goes UP
print(change_after_step([-g[0], -g[1]]))    # -0.88: against it, loss goes DOWN
print(change_after_step([1, 0]))            # -0.39: along w1 only

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: from (1, 3) take a step of size 0.1. Along the gradient direction the loss rises by about 0.91, against it falls by about 0.88, and along w1 only it falls by about 0.39. Both gradient moves are close to the gradient length 8.9 times the step 0.1, which is 0.89; the small difference is the curve bending.

quickCheck.explanation: The gradient points uphill, so the fastest way down is the exact opposite direction: [−3, 2].
options: Move along [3, −2]
Move along [2, 3]
Move along [3, 2]
Move along [−3, 2]
quickCheck.question: At the current weights the gradient of the loss is [3, −2]. Which move lowers the loss fastest?

theory.body: A partial derivative gives the slope along one knob. The gradient bundles all of them into one vector: ∇L = [∂L/∂w1, ∂L/∂w2]. For L(w1, w2) = (w1 − 3)² + 2(w2 − 1)² at (1, 3) that is [−4, 8]. It has one entry per weight, and it lives in the same space as the weights, so it can be drawn as an arrow from the current point.
theory.heading: Bundle the partial derivatives

theory.body: Of all directions you could step from here, the gradient points the way the loss increases fastest, and its length says how steep that climb is. Here the length is about 8.9 (the square root of 16 + 64). A long gradient means the ground is steep; a short one means it is nearly flat.
theory.heading: It points uphill, steepest

theory.body: To lower the loss as fast as possible, step opposite the gradient: −∇L = [4, −8]. That says move w1 up a bit and w2 down a lot, which matches what each partial derivative told us separately. Gradient descent is this single idea repeated.
theory.heading: Go the opposite way to go down

theory.body: Try several steps of the same small size from (1, 3): one along the gradient, one against it, one along w1 only. The step against the gradient lowers the loss the most. The step along the gradient raises it the most. Sideways steps land in between.
theory.heading: Test it yourself

theory.body: The minimum of this loss is at (3, 1), which from (1, 3) is the direction [2, −2]. The negative gradient [4, −8] is steeper in w2 because that direction is more sensitive. The gradient only knows the local slope, not where the bottom is. That is fine: you recompute it at every new point.
theory.heading: Steepest is not the same as straight at the minimum

checkpoints.subtitle: From a curve to a surface to a model with a thousand weights
checkpoints.title: Multivariate Functions

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: with w = [0, 0, 0], x = [1, 2, 3] and y = 6, the prediction error is 0 − 6 = −6. The gradient is 2 × (−6) × [1, 2, 3] = [−12, −24, −36]. All entries are negative, so every weight should increase, and the third (whose input is largest) should move the most.

quickCheck.explanation: The loss is one number, but the gradient has an entry for every weight, because each weight has its own partial derivative. The rules are the same in any number of dimensions.
options: 1,000: one partial derivative for each weight
1, because the loss is a single number
2: a slope and a curvature
None. Gradients can only be found for up to 3 weights
quickCheck.question: A model has 1,000 weights. How many entries does the gradient of its loss have?

theory.body: With one weight, the loss is a curve: weight along the bottom, loss as the height. This is the picture from the earlier checkpoints, such as L(w) = (w − 3)².
theory.heading: One variable: a curve

theory.body: Add a second weight and the loss becomes a surface. Every point on the floor is a pair (w1, w2), and the height above it is the loss. L(w1, w2) = (w1 − 3)² + 2(w2 − 1)² is a bowl with its lowest point above (3, 1). Standing on this surface, you can feel a slope in each of two directions.
theory.heading: Two variables: a surface

theory.body: Looking straight down on that bowl, all the points with the same loss form a loop, like contour lines on a hiking map. These loops are called level sets. Close-together loops mean steep ground. The gradient at any point is perpendicular to the loop through it, pointing across to the next-higher loop.
theory.heading: Contours show the surface from above

theory.body: Real models have not two weights but thousands or millions. We cannot draw that surface, but the rules do not change: the weights form a parameter vector w = [w1, w2, …, wn], the loss L(w) is still one number, and the gradient is still a list with one partial derivative per weight.
theory.heading: Many variables: same ideas, bigger list

theory.body: Let prediction = w1×x1 + w2×x2 + w3×x3 with inputs x = [1, 2, 3], target y = 6, and weights all starting at 0. The prediction is 0 and the loss (prediction − y)² is 36. Each partial derivative is 2 × (prediction − y) × its input, giving the gradient [−12, −24, −36]. Bigger inputs have bigger influence on the loss.
theory.heading: A small model with three weights

checkpoints.subtitle: Using the slope and the bend to predict a function near a point
checkpoints.title: Taylor Approximation

codeExamples.code:
def f(x):
    return x ** 3

def f_slope(x):
    return 3 * x ** 2

def f_curvature(x):
    return 6 * x

a = 1.0
for x in [1.2, 1.5, 2.0]:
    first = f(a) + f_slope(a) * (x - a)
    second = first + 0.5 * f_curvature(a) * (x - a) ** 2
    print(x, round(f(x), 3), round(first, 3), round(second, 3))
# 1.2 1.728 1.6 1.72
# 1.5 3.375 2.5 3.25
# 2.0 8.0 4.0 7.0

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: f(x) = x³ near a = 1. At x = 1.2: true 1.728, first order 1.6, second order 1.72. At x = 1.5: true 3.375, first order 2.5, second order 3.25. Adding the curvature term closes most of the gap, and the closer x is to a, the better both approximations are.

quickCheck.explanation: The first-order term already holds the value and the slope. The second-order term adds curvature, how quickly the slope changes, so the approximation follows the bend instead of staying straight.
options: The value of the function at the point
The slope at the point
How the slope is changing, which is the bend of the curve
The average of the training data
quickCheck.question: Compared with a straight tangent line, what does the second-order term in a Taylor approximation capture?

theory.body: Take a curved function f(x) = x³ and the point a = 1, where f(1) = 1. We want a simple formula that predicts f near a without computing the whole function. Taylor approximation builds one in layers: first the value, then the slope, then the bend.
theory.heading: A curve to approximate

theory.body: Using the value and the slope: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a). Here f'(x) = 3x², so f'(1) = 3 and the approximation is 1 + 3(x − 1). This is the straight-line approximation from the earlier checkpoint.
theory.heading: First order: the tangent line

theory.body: At x = 1.5 the true value is 3.375, but the tangent line gives 1 + 3 × 0.5 = 2.5. It is off by 0.875 because the real curve is bending upward and the line is not. At x = 2 the line says 4 while the truth is 8.
theory.heading: Where first order falls short

theory.body: Curvature is how fast the slope itself is changing, measured by the second derivative f''. Here f''(x) = 6x, so f''(1) = 6: the slope is growing. Add the term ½ × f''(a) × (x − a)². At x = 1.5 that is ½ × 6 × 0.25 = 0.75, giving 2.5 + 0.75 = 3.25, much closer to 3.375. At x = 2 you get 1 + 3 + 3 = 7 instead of 4.
theory.heading: Second order adds the bend

theory.body: A gradient alone is a first-order picture: it knows the slope but not how quickly the slope changes. Curvature tells you how far a gradient step stays trustworthy, and it is the extra information that second-order training methods use. With many weights the curvature becomes a table of second derivatives (called the Hessian); the idea is the same.
theory.heading: Why a model cares

checkpoints.title: Why Gradients Matter in ML

codeExamples.code:
x, y = 2, 6
w = 0.0
eta = 0.05            # the learning rate

for step in range(5):
    prediction = w * x
    loss = (prediction - y) ** 2
    gradient = 2 * (prediction - y) * x     # d loss / d w
    print(step, round(w, 3), round(loss, 3), round(gradient, 3))
    w = w - eta * gradient                  # step AGAINST the gradient
# 0 0.0 36.0 -24.0
# 1 1.2 12.96 -14.4
# 2 1.92 4.666 -8.64
# 3 2.352 1.68 -5.184
# 4 2.611 0.605 -3.11

workspace.learnMore: Worked example with η = 0.05, starting at w = 0: weights 0, 1.2, 1.92, 2.352, 2.611, … with losses 36, 12.96, 4.666, 1.68, 0.605, … Each loss is about 0.36 times the last, so the loss shrinks fast toward 0 and w approaches 3.

quickCheck.explanation: w − η × (−24) = w + 24η, so w goes up. A negative gradient means the loss falls as w rises, and the update follows that direction.
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It becomes −24
quickCheck.question: In the update w ← w − η × gradient, the gradient at the current w is −24. What happens to w?

theory.body: Let the model be prediction = w × x. Take input x = 2 and the true answer y = 6. The best weight would be 3, since 3 × 2 = 6. We start with w = 0, so the model predicts 0. This is the whole training problem in miniature.
theory.heading: A model with one weight

theory.body: Measure the miss with the squared error: loss = (prediction − y)². At w = 0 the loss is (0 − 6)² = 36. Training means finding the w that makes this number small.
theory.heading: The loss measures the miss

theory.body: The slope of the loss with respect to w is 2 × (prediction − y) × x. At w = 0 that is 2 × (−6) × 2 = −24. It is negative, so raising w lowers the loss, and large in size, so the loss is steep here.
theory.heading: The gradient points the way

theory.body: Move the weight a small step against the gradient: w ← w − η × gradient, where η (the learning rate) sets the step size. With η = 0.05, w becomes 0 − 0.05 × (−24) = 1.2, and the loss drops from 36 to 12.96. Repeat: the gradient is now −14.4, w becomes 1.92, and the loss is about 4.67.
theory.heading: The update rule

theory.body: Each step computes a new gradient at the new weight and moves again. The gradients shrink (−24, −14.4, −8.6, …) so the steps shrink too, and w settles near 3 where the gradient is zero and the loss is zero. A learning rate that is too big would overshoot and bounce. This predict, measure, differentiate, update loop is how nearly all of machine learning is trained.
theory.heading: Repeat until the slope fades

checkpoints.subtitle: Naming what could happen, and how much each possibility counts
checkpoints.title: Probability Spaces

codeExamples.code:
outcomes = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
p = {o: 1 / 6 for o in outcomes}           # a fair die

even = [o for o in outcomes if o % 2 == 0]
at_least_5 = [o for o in outcomes if o >= 5]

print(round(sum(p[o] for o in even), 3))        # 0.5
print(round(sum(p[o] for o in at_least_5), 3))  # 0.333
print(round(sum(p.values()), 3))                # 1.0: all outcomes add to 1

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: with 1/6 on each face, P(at least 5) = 2/6 = 1/3, and P(not even) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. Giving every face 0.2 is not valid, because six faces would add up to 1.2.

quickCheck.explanation: The event is {5, 6}: two outcomes, each with probability 1/6, so the event has probability 2/6 = 1/3.
quickCheck.question: You roll a fair six-sided die. What is the probability of the event 'the roll is at least 5'?

theory.body: Machine learning deals with things we cannot know for sure: whether an email is spam, what a house will sell for, what a sensor will read. Probability gives uncertainty a precise language. We start with the simplest uncertain thing, a roll of a fair six-sided die: before the roll, you cannot say which face will come up.
theory.heading: Uncertainty needs a precise language

theory.body: A random experiment is any process whose result is uncertain. Each possible result is an outcome. The set of all possible outcomes is the sample space. For one die roll the outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Exactly one outcome happens each time.
theory.heading: Outcomes and the sample space

theory.body: An event is any collection of outcomes we care about. 'The roll is even' is the event {2, 4, 6}. 'The roll is at least 5' is the event {5, 6}. An event happens when the actual outcome is one of its members.
theory.heading: Events

theory.body: A probability is a number from 0 (cannot happen) to 1 (certain). For a fair die each outcome gets 1/6. The probability of an event is the sum of its outcomes: P(even) = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/2. An assignment is valid when every probability is between 0 and 1 and the probabilities of all the mutually exclusive outcomes add up to exactly 1, because something must happen.
theory.heading: Probabilities attach to outcomes and events

theory.body: A classifier that outputs spam 0.9 and not spam 0.1 is giving a probability assignment over its two possible outcomes. If those numbers did not add up to 1 they would not describe a coherent belief. Everything later in this module, from conditioning to the Gaussian, builds on this foundation.
theory.heading: Why it matters for ML

checkpoints.subtitle: How new information changes the denominator
checkpoints.title: Conditional Probability

codeExamples.code:
# 100 emails as counts: (is_spam, has_free) -> how many
counts = {
    (True, True): 24,
    (True, False): 16,
    (False, True): 6,
    (False, False): 54,
}
total = sum(counts.values())
spam = counts[(True, True)] + counts[(True, False)]
free = counts[(True, True)] + counts[(False, True)]

print(spam / total)                  # 0.4  P(spam)
print(counts[(True, True)] / free)   # 0.8  P(spam | free): denominator is 'free' only
print(counts[(True, True)] / spam)   # 0.6  P(free | spam): a different question

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: the 100 emails split as 24 spam with 'free', 16 spam without, 6 not-spam with 'free' and 54 not-spam without. Spam total 40, 'free' total 30, so P(spam | free) = 24/30 and P(free | spam) = 24/40.

quickCheck.explanation: Conditioning on 'free' restricts attention to the 30 emails that contain it, so the denominator becomes 30 instead of 100.
options: 24 / 30 = 0.8, because we only count the emails containing 'free'
24 / 100 = 0.24, because we always divide by all emails
30 / 100 = 0.3, the share of emails containing 'free'
40 / 100 = 0.4, the share of spam overall
quickCheck.question: Among 100 emails, 30 contain 'free' and 24 of those are spam. What is P(spam | free)?

theory.body: Imagine 100 emails, of which 40 are spam. Pick one at random: P(spam) = 40/100 = 0.4. Now suppose you learn the email contains the word 'free'. That changes the question. You are no longer picking from all 100 emails, only from the ones containing 'free'.
theory.heading: Information changes what is possible

theory.body: Say 30 of the 100 emails contain 'free', and 24 of those 30 are spam. Restrict attention to those 30. Inside that smaller group, spam makes up 24 of 30, which is 0.8. The probability of spam given 'free' is 0.8, double the original 0.4.
theory.heading: Restrict, then count again

theory.body: We write this P(spam | free), read 'the probability of spam given free'. In general P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), whenever P(B) is greater than 0. Here P(spam and free) = 24/100 and P(free) = 30/100, so the ratio is 0.24 / 0.30 = 0.8. The key move is the denominator: it changed from everything to just B.
theory.heading: The notation and the formula

theory.body: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different questions. Here P(free | spam) = 24/40 = 0.6: among spam emails, 60% contain 'free'. But P(spam | free) = 0.8. Mixing the two up is one of the most common mistakes in probability, and the next checkpoint is built on telling them apart.
theory.heading: Order matters

theory.body: Every prediction is conditional. A classifier does not ask 'is this spam?' in a vacuum; it asks 'is this spam, given these words, this sender, this link?'. Conditional probability is how evidence enters a model.
theory.heading: Why it matters for ML

workspace.title: Conditional Probability

checkpoints.subtitle: Updating a belief after seeing evidence
checkpoints.title: Bayes Rule

codeExamples.code:
prior = 0.4          # P(spam)
like_spam = 0.6      # P(free | spam)
like_ham = 0.1       # P(free | not spam)

evidence = like_spam * prior + like_ham * (1 - prior)   # P(free)
posterior = like_spam * prior / evidence                # P(spam | free)
print(round(evidence, 2), round(posterior, 2))          # 0.3 0.8

# the same evidence is much weaker when spam is rare
rare_prior = 0.01
rare_evidence = like_spam * rare_prior + like_ham * (1 - rare_prior)
print(round(like_spam * rare_prior / rare_evidence, 3)) # 0.057

workspace.learnMore: Worked example of why the prior matters: the same evidence ('free', with the same likelihoods 0.6 and 0.1) applied to a prior of only P(spam) = 0.01 gives a posterior of 0.6 × 0.01 / (0.6 × 0.01 + 0.1 × 0.99) = 0.006 / 0.105, about 0.057. A strong clue is not the same as a strong conclusion when the thing is rare.

quickCheck.explanation: Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence = 0.9 × 0.2 / 0.3 = 0.18 / 0.3 = 0.6. The evidence raised the belief from 0.2 to 0.6.
quickCheck.question: A filter has prior P(spam) = 0.2, likelihood P(free | spam) = 0.9, and overall P(free) = 0.3. What is the posterior P(spam | free)?

theory.body: Before opening an email you already have a belief about it: 40% of your mail is spam, so P(spam) = 0.4. This starting belief is the prior. Then you see evidence, the word 'free'. Bayes' rule is the recipe for how far that evidence should move your belief.
theory.heading: Belief before and after evidence

theory.body: From past emails it is easy to measure how often spam contains 'free': P(free | spam) = 0.6. This is the likelihood: how likely the evidence is if the email is spam. But what you want is the reverse, P(spam | free): the chance the email is spam given that you see 'free'. The condition has flipped direction.
theory.heading: What you know vs. what you want

theory.body: Bayes' rule reverses the condition: P(spam | free) = P(free | spam) × P(spam) / P(free). In words: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. The posterior is the updated belief after the evidence.
theory.heading: The rule

theory.body: P(free) is the total chance of seeing 'free' from any source, spam or not spam: P(free) = 0.6 × 0.4 + 0.1 × 0.6 = 0.24 + 0.06 = 0.30 (here 0.1 is P(free | not spam), and 0.6 is P(not spam)). Dividing by it makes the competing explanations share the evidence fairly, so the posteriors add up to 1.
theory.heading: The evidence term normalizes

theory.body: P(spam | free) = 0.6 × 0.4 / 0.30 = 0.24 / 0.30 = 0.8. The belief moved from 0.4 to 0.8, the same answer as counting in the last checkpoint, now built from pieces a model can estimate: a prior and likelihoods. Probabilistic classifiers such as naive Bayes work exactly this way, and Bayesian inference later in the course is the same update applied to model parameters.
theory.heading: The result, and why ML cares
