checkpoints.title: Split the Data

codeExamples.code:
n = 1000
customers = [{"id": i, "week": i // 50 + 1} for i in range(n)]    # 50 observations per week, weeks 1-20
train = [c for c in customers if c["week"] <= 14]
valid = [c for c in customers if 15 <= c["week"] <= 17]
test = [c for c in customers if c["week"] >= 18]
print("train / validation / test:", len(train), len(valid), len(test))

ids = [{c["id"] for c in part} for part in (train, valid, test)]
print("overlap between the sets:", len(ids[0] & ids[1]) + len(ids[0] & ids[2]) + len(ids[1] & ids[2]))
print("newest training week:", max(c["week"] for c in train), " earliest validation week:", min(c["week"] for c in valid))

# a random-looking split of the same customers mixes the weeks together
shuffled = [customers[(i * 37) % n] for i in range(n)]
r_train, r_valid = shuffled[:700], shuffled[700:850]
newest = max(c["week"] for c in r_train)
print("validation customers observed before the newest training customer:")
print("  chronological split:", sum(c["week"] < max(t["week"] for t in train) for c in valid))
print("  random split:", sum(c["week"] < newest for c in r_valid))
test_opened = False       # the test set stays locked until the final evaluation
print("test set opened during development:", test_opened)

# Output:
# train / validation / test: 700 150 150
# overlap between the sets: 0
# newest training week: 14  earliest validation week: 15
# validation customers observed before the newest training customer:
#   chronological split: 0
#   random split: 144
# test set opened during development: False

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: 1,000 customers are observed at 50 per week for 20 weeks. The chronological split gives 700 / 150 / 150 with no overlap, and every validation customer is observed after the newest training customer. A random split of the same customers puts nearly all of the 150 validation customers earlier than the newest training customer, which means the model has seen the future of the customers it is judged on.

quickCheck.explanation: Training fits the parameters, validation guides every choice, and the test set is opened once, after the choices are locked. Anything that uses the test set to decide makes the final estimate optimistic.
options: Tune settings on the test set, then report the validation score
Fit parameters on all data, then split it to measure the result
Use the test set to pick the best of several models, then retrain on it
Fit parameters on the training set, choose models and settings with the validation set, and evaluate once on the test set at the end
quickCheck.question: Which workflow uses the three data sets correctly?

theory.body: Our churn project has 1,000 customer observations. We split them into 700 for training, 150 for validation and 150 for testing. Training data is used to fit the model's parameters. Validation data is used to choose between models, settings and thresholds. Test data gives one final estimate after every choice is locked.
theory.heading: Three sets, three jobs

theory.body: Make the split before exploring results and before choosing anything. Each time we look at a score and then change something, the data behind that score influences our decisions. If we use the test set that way, it stops being a fair estimate of new data.
theory.heading: Split before you look

theory.body: While we develop, the test set is not opened. No tuning, no peeking, no "just checking". If it is opened and used to make a choice, the final number is optimistic, and there is no untouched data left to measure how optimistic it is.
theory.heading: The test set stays locked

theory.body: Churn prediction is about the future. If observations are spread over 20 weeks, a random split mixes weeks together, so a model may train on customers observed after some of the customers it is validated on. A chronological split is safer here: weeks 1 to 14 for training (700), weeks 15 to 17 for validation (150), weeks 18 to 20 for testing (150), so the model is always evaluated on later data.
theory.heading: Respect time

theory.body: A split does not make a model good. It makes our measurements honest. A random split is fine for data without time structure. Here the choice depends on how the model will be used: it will predict forward in time, so the evaluation should do the same.
theory.heading: What a split protects

workspace.title: Split the Data

checkpoints.subtitle: Start simple and justify every step up in complexity
checkpoints.title: Choose a Model

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: the baseline rule on 150 validation customers has 12 true positives, 10 false positives, 18 false negatives and 110 true negatives. Accuracy is (12 + 110) / 150 = 0.813, precision is 12 / 22 = 0.545 and recall is 12 / 30 = 0.40. It looks respectable by accuracy and misses most churners, so the target for a model is to improve recall without wasting too many contacts.

quickCheck.explanation: With 20% churners, a do-nothing rule scores 0.80 accuracy. Accuracy differences of two points say little about catching churners. Compare against the baseline on the metrics that match the goal, here recall and precision.
options: Check recall and precision for the churn class and compare against the baseline, because accuracy hides how many churners are missed
Ship the complex model, because any improvement in accuracy is enough
Discard the baseline, because simple rules cannot be compared with models
Choose the complex model because it has more parameters
quickCheck.question: A team has a rule that already scores 0.81 accuracy on churn data where 20% of customers churn. A complex model scores 0.83. What is the best response?

theory.body: Churn is a binary classification problem: each customer is churn (1) or not (0). That narrows the choice to classifiers. Within that family we choose by data size, interpretability, complexity and constraints such as speed, not by fashion.
theory.heading: Match the tool to the problem

theory.body: A baseline is the simplest reasonable approach. For us it is a rule: flag a customer who has been inactive for more than 30 days. On the validation set it flags 22 customers and catches 12 of the 30 churners: accuracy 0.813 but recall only 0.40. Any model must beat this, and judging by recall rather than accuracy.
theory.heading: Start with a baseline

theory.body: Two natural candidates are a logistic-style linear classifier, which weighs each feature and is easy to explain, and a tree-style model, which asks a sequence of yes/no questions about features and can capture interactions. Neither is chosen in advance. They are hypotheses we will train and measure.
theory.heading: Candidates, not winners

theory.body: A more flexible model can fit more patterns, including accidental ones. It is also harder to explain, slower to tune and easier to overfit. Add complexity only when simpler models fall short on the criterion we set in the framing.
theory.heading: More complex is not automatically better

theory.body: Ours: churn staff need to understand why a customer was flagged (interpretability), the model scores customers once a day (speed is not critical), and we have 700 training examples (modest). These point to simple, explainable models first, and we will compare them fairly on the validation set.
theory.heading: Write down the constraints

workspace.title: Choose a Model

checkpoints.subtitle: Adjusting parameters on the training data to lower the loss
checkpoints.title: Train the Model

codeExamples.code:
import math

days = [2, 5, 8, 12, 20, 25, 30, 35]        # toy training customers: days since last activity
churn = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1]
x = [d / 10 for d in days]                  # scaled feature
w, b = 0.0, 0.0                             # parameters: learned from the training data
lr = 0.5                                    # learning rate: a hyperparameter WE choose

def predict(xi):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-(w * xi + b)))

def loss():
    return -sum(y * math.log(predict(xi)) + (1 - y) * math.log(1 - predict(xi)) for xi, y in zip(x, churn)) / len(x)

print("start: loss", round(loss(), 4), "w", w, "b", b)
for step in range(1, 6):
    errors = [predict(xi) - y for xi, y in zip(x, churn)]
    grad_w = sum(e * xi for e, xi in zip(errors, x)) / len(x)
    grad_b = sum(errors) / len(x)
    w, b = w - lr * grad_w, b - lr * grad_b
    print("step", step, ": loss", round(loss(), 4), "w", round(w, 3), "b", round(b, 3))

# Output:
# start: loss 0.6931 w 0.0 b 0.0
# step 1 : loss 0.6674 w 0.103 b -0.062
# step 2 : loss 0.6487 w 0.165 b -0.139
# step 3 : loss 0.6318 w 0.211 b -0.219
# step 4 : loss 0.6162 w 0.251 b -0.299
# step 5 : loss 0.6016 w 0.287 b -0.378

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: with weight 0 and bias 0 the model predicts 0.5 for everyone and the loss is about 0.693 (the log of 2). After each gradient step the weight on days-inactive grows, because longer inactivity goes with churn, and the loss falls. Training stops here after a fixed number of steps; in practice we also watch whether the loss has stopped improving.

quickCheck.explanation: Training updates parameters (weights and bias) by following the loss gradient on training data. The learning rate is a chosen setting, and validation and test labels are not used to update parameters.
options: The validation labels are used in each step so that the loss reflects unseen data
The learning rate is learned automatically from the training data by the same loop
The test set is checked every few steps to decide when to stop
The parameters are updated using the training data to reduce the loss, while the learning rate is a setting chosen by us
quickCheck.question: During training of the churn model, which statement is correct?

theory.body: Training adjusts the model's parameters using the training data so that an objective, the loss, gets smaller. A logistic-style churn model has a weight for each feature and a bias. At the start they are arbitrary, so the predictions are poor and the loss is high.
theory.heading: What training changes

theory.body: Training repeats four moves: make predictions with the current parameters, measure the loss against the true labels, compute the gradient (the direction in which the loss rises fastest), and move the parameters a small step the opposite way. This is the gradient descent from the optimization lessons, applied to our churn labels.
theory.heading: The loop

theory.body: The weights and bias are parameters: they are learned from the data. The learning rate, the size of each step, is not learned by this loop. We choose it, and a poor choice makes training slow or unstable. That difference returns when we tune hyperparameters.
theory.heading: Parameters and learning rate

theory.body: The loop uses the training set and nothing else. The validation set is for judging the finished model and comparing choices. If validation labels were used to update the parameters, the validation score would stop being an honest check.
theory.heading: Training data only

theory.body: The example below trains a one-feature churn model on 8 toy customers, not the full 700, with plain Python. The loss falls at each step while the weight and bias change. Real libraries add speed and care but do the same thing.
theory.heading: A toy you can run

workspace.title: Train the Model

checkpoints.subtitle: Choosing the evaluation view that fits the goal
checkpoints.title: Evaluate Performance

codeExamples.code:
# validation confusion matrices, positive class = churn: (TP, FP, FN, TN), 150 validation customers
VAL = {"baseline": (12, 10, 18, 110), "logistic": (21, 12, 9, 108), "tree": (24, 17, 6, 103)}
def metrics(tp, fp, fn, tn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn)
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return {"accuracy": (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn), "precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1}
def meets_goal(m):      # the stated goal: catch at least 75% of churners with precision of at least 50%
    return m["recall"] >= 0.75 and m["precision"] >= 0.50

tp, fp, fn, tn = VAL["logistic"]
print("confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN):", (tp, fp, fn, tn), " total:", tp + fp + fn + tn)
m = metrics(tp, fp, fn, tn)
for name in ("accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"):
    print(name, round(m[name], 3))
print("meets the stated goal:", meets_goal(m))
print("baseline accuracy for comparison:", round(metrics(*VAL["baseline"])["accuracy"], 3))

# Output:
# confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN): (21, 12, 9, 108)  total: 150
# accuracy 0.86
# precision 0.636
# recall 0.7
# f1 0.667
# meets the stated goal: False
# baseline accuracy for comparison: 0.813

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: for the logistic-style model, precision = 21 / (21 + 12) = 0.636, recall = 21 / (21 + 9) = 0.70, F1 = 2 × 0.636 × 0.70 / (0.636 + 0.70) = 0.667 and accuracy = (21 + 108) / 150 = 0.86. Against the goal (recall ≥ 0.75, precision ≥ 0.50) it passes precision and misses recall.

quickCheck.explanation: The two kinds of mistake have different costs, so look at precision and recall together against the framed goal. Accuracy hides the minority class, and the training and test scores are not the right tools for development decisions.
options: Accuracy alone, because it counts all correct predictions
The confusion matrix with precision and recall together, judged against the stated goal
Only the training score, because validation is noisy
Only the test score, to avoid bias
quickCheck.question: Retention staff can contact only a limited number of customers, and each wasted contact costs money, but missing a churner loses the customer for good. Which view of the validation results is most useful?

theory.body: After training, we measure the first candidate, the logistic-style model, on the 150 validation customers it has not trained on. Churn is the positive class. The confusion matrix counts four outcomes: 21 true positives (churners caught), 12 false positives (contacted but would have stayed), 9 false negatives (churners missed) and 108 true negatives.
theory.heading: Evaluate on validation data

theory.body: From these counts: accuracy 0.86, precision 0.636 (of the customers we flag, how many really churn), recall 0.70 (of the real churners, how many we catch) and F1 0.667 (their harmonic mean). No single number tells the whole story.
theory.heading: Read several metrics

theory.body: Our goal was recall of at least 0.75 with precision of at least 0.50. If missing a churner is costly because an offer could have kept them, recall matters most. If contacting too many people is expensive, precision matters. This model has recall 0.70, below the goal, even though its accuracy of 0.86 looks good.
theory.heading: Let the goal choose the view

theory.body: The baseline has accuracy 0.81 and the model 0.86, a small difference, yet recall rose from 0.40 to 0.70. With 20% churners, accuracy is dominated by the many customers who stay.
theory.heading: Accuracy can flatter

theory.body: These numbers come from validation data and guide development. The test set is still locked. Evaluation here is a measurement of the current candidate against the goal, and the next lessons ask what to do when it falls short.
theory.heading: Validation, not test

workspace.title: Evaluate Performance

checkpoints.subtitle: Poor on training data and poor on validation data
checkpoints.title: Diagnose Underfitting

codeExamples.code:
# toy tuning results for the tree-style model: (max_depth, train F1, validation F1)
RESULTS = [(1, 0.48, 0.46), (2, 0.62, 0.58), (4, 0.76, 0.676), (8, 0.97, 0.59)]

def diagnose(train, valid):
    gap = train - valid
    if train < 0.65 and valid < 0.65 and gap < 0.10:
        return "underfitting: weak on both sets"
    if gap > 0.20:
        return "overfitting: strong on training, much weaker on validation"
    return "no clear fit problem"

for depth, train, valid in RESULTS:
    print("depth", depth, ": train", train, "validation", valid, "gap", round(train - valid, 2), "->", diagnose(train, valid))
print("possible fixes:", ["better features", "more suitable model", "check training converged", "revisit the framing"])

# Output:
# depth 1 : train 0.48 validation 0.46 gap 0.02 -> underfitting: weak on both sets
# depth 2 : train 0.62 validation 0.58 gap 0.04 -> underfitting: weak on both sets
# depth 4 : train 0.76 validation 0.676 gap 0.08 -> no clear fit problem
# depth 8 : train 0.97 validation 0.59 gap 0.38 -> overfitting: strong on training, much weaker on validation
# possible fixes: ['better features', 'more suitable model', 'check training converged', 'revisit the framing']

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: depth 1 has train F1 0.48 and validation F1 0.46, a gap of only 0.02. Depth 2 reaches 0.62 and 0.58. Both are well below the F1 of about 0.67 that the goal needs, and the small gap between training and validation says the shortfall is not caused by memorizing the training data: the model is not fitting the pattern yet.

quickCheck.explanation: Poor scores on both sets point to underfitting. Close scores only show there is little overfitting; they say nothing about whether the model is good enough. Check the model, features and training before changing anything else.
options: The model is overfitting, so regularization should be increased
The test set should be used to find out what is wrong
The model is probably too simple or the features too weak, since it performs poorly even on data it trained on
The model is fine, because the two scores are close
quickCheck.question: A churn model scores 0.48 F1 on training data and 0.46 on validation data. Which conclusion is best supported?

theory.body: Compare the score on training data with the score on validation data. If both are poor, the model has not captured the pattern even where it was allowed to learn it. We call this underfitting. Our tree-style model with a maximum depth of 1 has an F1 of 0.48 on training data and 0.46 on validation data: weak on both.
theory.heading: The pattern

theory.body: A depth-1 tree asks one question, so its decision boundary is a single straight cut through the feature space. The churn pattern needs several signals together (long inactivity, many tickets, short tenure), and one cut cannot express that. Training performance is poor because the model cannot represent the pattern.
theory.heading: What the picture looks like

theory.body: A model that is too simple is one cause. Others: the features carry little information about churn, training stopped too early or used a bad learning rate, the label is very noisy, or the problem was represented in a way that hides the signal. Underfitting is a symptom, and the cause needs checking.
theory.heading: Several possible causes

theory.body: Try a more suitable model or more flexibility, add or improve features, make sure training actually converged, or revisit the framing and the target. Collecting more data of the same kind rarely helps a model that cannot even fit the training data it has.
theory.heading: Possible fixes

theory.body: Low scores on both sets suggest underfitting but do not prove a single cause. We still need to look at the features and training. After a change we measure again on validation data, never on the test set.
theory.heading: Diagnosis is evidence

workspace.title: Diagnose Underfitting

checkpoints.subtitle: Strong on training data, clearly weaker on validation data
checkpoints.title: Diagnose Overfitting

codeExamples.code:
# toy tuning results for the tree-style model: (max_depth, train F1, validation F1)
RESULTS = [(1, 0.48, 0.46), (2, 0.62, 0.58), (4, 0.76, 0.676), (8, 0.97, 0.59)]

for depth, train, valid in RESULTS:
    print("depth", depth, ": train", train, " validation", valid, " gap", round(train - valid, 3))

worst = max(RESULTS, key=lambda r: r[1] - r[2])
print("largest train-validation gap at depth", worst[0], ":", round(worst[1] - worst[2], 2))
best_valid = max(RESULTS, key=lambda r: r[2])
print("best validation score at depth", best_valid[0], ":", best_valid[2])

checks = ["is any feature leaking the outcome?", "is the model too complex for 700 customers?", "is the validation set being over-used for tuning?"]
for question in checks:
    print("check:", question)

# Output:
# depth 1 : train 0.48  validation 0.46  gap 0.02
# depth 2 : train 0.62  validation 0.58  gap 0.04
# depth 4 : train 0.76  validation 0.676  gap 0.084
# depth 8 : train 0.97  validation 0.59  gap 0.38
# largest train-validation gap at depth 8 : 0.38
# best validation score at depth 4 : 0.676
# check: is any feature leaking the outcome?
# check: is the model too complex for 700 customers?
# check: is the validation set being over-used for tuning?

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: the training-validation gaps for the tree are 0.02 (depth 1), 0.04 (depth 2), 0.084 (depth 4) and 0.38 (depth 8). The validation score rises from 0.46 to 0.676 as the model gets more flexible, then falls to 0.59 at depth 8 while training keeps climbing. Choosing the depth with the best validation score, depth 4, is the next lesson.

quickCheck.explanation: A big gap is evidence of overfitting, not proof of one cause. Check for leakage and noise, try regularization or a simpler model, and re-evaluate on validation data.
options: A large train-validation gap suggests overfitting, but leakage or noisy features could also contribute, so check them while trying a simpler or regularized model
The model is certainly overfitting because of its depth, and nothing else needs to be checked
The training F1 shows the model is excellent
The validation score is unreliable, so the training score should be reported
quickCheck.question: A deep tree has training F1 0.97 and validation F1 0.59. What is the most accurate statement?

theory.body: Now let the churn model's tree grow to a maximum depth of 8. Its F1 on training data jumps to 0.97, while on validation data it falls to 0.59, lower than the depth-4 tree's 0.676. A large gap with strong training results is the signature of overfitting: the model has fitted details of the training customers that do not carry over.
theory.heading: The pattern

theory.body: Excessive complexity for the amount of data is the classic cause: A deep tree can memorize which of our 700 training customers churned. Leakage can also produce a strong training score that collapses elsewhere. Other causes are noisy features, too little data for the model's flexibility, and over-tuning against the same validation data.
theory.heading: Possible causes

theory.body: Use regularization, which penalizes complexity just as ridge regression penalizes large weights. Use a simpler model or a smaller depth. Clean up noisy features and check for leakage. Use a better validation scheme, and add useful training data where that is possible.
theory.heading: Possible remedies

theory.body: A gap of 0.38 between training and validation F1 tells us something is wrong. It does not by itself tell us which cause applies, and it does not prove the model is useless. We form a hypothesis, change one thing, and measure again on validation data.
theory.heading: Evidence, not proof

theory.body: Underfitting: poor on both. Overfitting: strong on training, materially worse on validation. These descriptions are guides and not hard thresholds, and a model can show both problems in different parts of the data.
theory.heading: Compare the two failure modes

workspace.title: Diagnose Overfitting

checkpoints.subtitle: Choosing settings with validation data, not the test set
checkpoints.title: Tune Hyperparameters

codeExamples.code:
# toy tuning results for the tree-style model: (max_depth, train F1, validation F1)
RESULTS = [(1, 0.48, 0.46), (2, 0.62, 0.58), (4, 0.76, 0.676), (8, 0.97, 0.59)]

test_used = False           # the test set must not take part in choosing a setting

print("hyperparameter: max_depth (chosen by us, not learned from the data)")
for depth, train, valid in RESULTS:
    print("  tried depth", depth, "-> validation F1", valid)

best_depth, best_train, best_valid = max(RESULTS, key=lambda r: r[2])      # select on VALIDATION
print("selected max_depth:", best_depth, " validation F1:", best_valid)
print("by training score we would wrongly pick depth:", max(RESULTS, key=lambda r: r[1])[0])
print("test set used for tuning:", test_used)

# Output:
# hyperparameter: max_depth (chosen by us, not learned from the data)
#   tried depth 1 -> validation F1 0.46
#   tried depth 2 -> validation F1 0.58
#   tried depth 4 -> validation F1 0.676
#   tried depth 8 -> validation F1 0.59
# selected max_depth: 4  validation F1: 0.676
# by training score we would wrongly pick depth: 8
# test set used for tuning: False

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: RESULTS = [(1, 0.48, 0.46), (2, 0.62, 0.58), (4, 0.76, 0.676), (8, 0.97, 0.59)]. Selecting by validation F1 gives depth 4 (0.676). Selecting by training F1 would give depth 8 (0.97), the overfitted model. The chosen depth 4 gives the tree-style model whose validation confusion matrix is 24 / 17 / 6 / 103 and whose recall is 0.80.

quickCheck.explanation: Hyperparameters such as depth are chosen using validation results. The best training score tends to favour overfitted settings, and using the test set to choose makes the final estimate optimistic.
options: Try several depths and keep the one with the best training score
Try several depths, fit each on the training set, choose the one with the best validation score, and leave the test set untouched until the end
Try several depths on the test set and report the best test score as the final result
Let the training loop learn the depth by gradient descent
quickCheck.question: Which description of tuning the tree depth is correct?

theory.body: Parameters, such as weights or the split values inside a tree, are learned from the training data. Hyperparameters are chosen outside that fitting process. Examples are the regularization strength, the maximum depth of a tree, the learning rate and the decision threshold for flagging a customer.
theory.heading: Parameters versus hyperparameters

theory.body: Pick candidate settings. For each one, train on the training data. Evaluate each trained model on the validation data. Compare the results and choose a setting. The validation set plays the judge, which is why it must be kept separate from the data used to fit parameters.
theory.heading: The tuning workflow

theory.body: For the churn model we try maximum depths 1, 2, 4 and 8. The validation F1 scores are 0.46, 0.58, 0.676 and 0.59. Depth 4 wins on validation. Notice that depth 8 has the best training score: the training score is not what we select on.
theory.heading: Our tree depth

theory.body: If we picked the depth with the best test score, the test set would have been used to make a choice, and its score would be optimistic. The test set stays locked until the model and its settings are final. Even validation can be over-used if we try a huge number of settings, so keep the search modest.
theory.heading: Do not tune on the test set

theory.body: A short, deliberate list of candidates is often enough. Plain Python and a loop over a few settings is a complete tuning procedure. Record which settings were tried and their scores, so the choice can be checked later.
theory.heading: Keep the churn search small and honest

workspace.title: Tune Hyperparameters

checkpoints.subtitle: Fair comparison on the same data, protocol and metrics
checkpoints.title: Compare Models

codeExamples.code:
# validation confusion matrices, positive class = churn: (TP, FP, FN, TN), 150 validation customers
VAL = {"baseline": (12, 10, 18, 110), "logistic": (21, 12, 9, 108), "tree": (24, 17, 6, 103)}
def metrics(tp, fp, fn, tn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn)
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return {"accuracy": (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn), "precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1}
def meets_goal(m):      # the stated goal: catch at least 75% of churners with precision of at least 50%
    return m["recall"] >= 0.75 and m["precision"] >= 0.50

print("same data, same protocol: 150 validation customers, positive class = churn")
passing = []
for name, counts in VAL.items():
    m = metrics(*counts)
    ok = meets_goal(m)
    print(name, "precision", round(m["precision"], 2), "recall", round(m["recall"], 2), "F1", round(m["f1"], 2), "meets goal:", ok)
    if ok:
        passing.append(name)

chosen = max(passing, key=lambda name: metrics(*VAL[name])["f1"])
print("candidates that meet the goal:", passing)
print("locked choice:", chosen, "(tree-style, max_depth 4)")
test_opened = False
print("test set opened so far:", test_opened)

# Output:
# same data, same protocol: 150 validation customers, positive class = churn
# baseline precision 0.55 recall 0.4 F1 0.46 meets goal: False
# logistic precision 0.64 recall 0.7 F1 0.67 meets goal: False
# tree precision 0.59 recall 0.8 F1 0.68 meets goal: True
# candidates that meet the goal: ['tree']
# locked choice: tree (tree-style, max_depth 4)
# test set opened so far: False

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: validation results (precision / recall / F1): baseline 0.55 / 0.40 / 0.46; logistic-style 0.64 / 0.70 / 0.67; tree-style (depth 4) 0.59 / 0.80 / 0.68. Only the tree-style model meets both parts of the goal. The comparison also shows a trade-off: it gives up some precision (0.64 to 0.59) to gain recall (0.70 to 0.80).

quickCheck.explanation: A fair comparison uses the same data, protocol and metrics for every candidate. Training scores flatter models and the test set should not drive model selection.
options: Nothing: each model is measured on the most relevant data
Models should be compared using only their parameter counts
The models were not evaluated under one protocol, so their scores are not comparable; all should use the same validation data and metrics, with the test set kept for the final check
Model Z should have been evaluated on the training data as well
quickCheck.question: Three models are compared. Model X is evaluated on the validation set, Model Y on its own training data, and Model Z on the test set. What is wrong with this comparison?

theory.body: Now compare the three candidates: the baseline rule, the logistic-style model and the tuned tree-style model (depth 4). They must use the same training data, the same validation set of 150 customers, and the same metrics. A comparison where each model is judged on different data or a different metric tells us little.
theory.heading: One fair protocol

theory.body: On validation data: the baseline has precision 0.55, recall 0.40 and F1 0.46. The logistic-style model has precision 0.64, recall 0.70 and F1 0.67. The tree-style model has precision 0.59, recall 0.80 and F1 0.68.
theory.heading: The metric table

theory.body: We framed success as recall of at least 0.75 with precision of at least 0.50. The baseline and the logistic model miss on recall. The tree-style model passes both: recall 0.80, precision 0.59. Its F1 is also the highest. The goal, not just the highest number, decides.
theory.heading: Return to the goal

theory.body: Metrics are not the whole decision. Compare simplicity, interpretability, speed and stability too. The tree is still small enough to explain, and daily scoring is cheap, so nothing outweighs its recall advantage. If two candidates were close, a simpler or more stable one might be preferred.
theory.heading: Other considerations

theory.body: Write down the chosen model, its settings (tree-style, maximum depth 4) and its decision rule. After this point nothing about the model changes. Only then is the model ready for a single evaluation on the test set.
theory.heading: Lock the choice

checkpoints.subtitle: Putting the whole loop together, from problem to monitored model
checkpoints.title: Final ML Workflow

codeExamples.code:
# validation confusion matrices, positive class = churn: (TP, FP, FN, TN), 150 validation customers
VAL = {"baseline": (12, 10, 18, 110), "logistic": (21, 12, 9, 108), "tree": (24, 17, 6, 103)}
def metrics(tp, fp, fn, tn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn)
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return {"accuracy": (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn), "precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1}
def meets_goal(m):      # the stated goal: catch at least 75% of churners with precision of at least 50%
    return m["recall"] >= 0.75 and m["precision"] >= 0.50

workflow = ["frame problem", "features and target", "check leakage", "split data", "baseline", "choose candidates",
            "train", "evaluate on validation", "diagnose fit", "tune hyperparameters", "compare candidates",
            "lock model and settings", "evaluate once on test", "document limits", "monitor after deployment"]
print(len(workflow), "steps, first:", workflow[0], "| last:", workflow[-1])

TEST = (22, 19, 6, 103)         # 150 test customers, evaluated ONCE after the choice was locked
val, test = metrics(*VAL["tree"]), metrics(*TEST)
print("validation F1:", round(val["f1"], 3), " test F1:", round(test["f1"], 3))
print("test precision:", round(test["precision"], 3), " recall:", round(test["recall"], 3))
print("still meets the goal on test:", meets_goal(test))

# toy monitoring example: has incoming data drifted from the training data? (15% is a teaching value, not a universal threshold)
train_usage, recent_usage, tolerance = 12.0, 9.0, 0.15
shift = (recent_usage - train_usage) / train_usage
print("usage shift since training:", round(shift, 2), "-> investigate:", abs(shift) > tolerance)

# Output:
# 15 steps, first: frame problem | last: monitor after deployment
# validation F1: 0.676  test F1: 0.638
# test precision: 0.537  recall: 0.786
# still meets the goal on test: True
# usage shift since training: -0.25 -> investigate: True

workspace.learnMore: Worked example: on the test set TP = 22, FP = 19, FN = 6, TN = 103, so precision = 22 / 41 = 0.537, recall = 22 / 28 = 0.786 and F1 = 0.638. Validation F1 was 0.676. As a toy monitoring example (the 15% tolerance is a teaching value, not a universal threshold), if average monthly usage was 12.0 hours in the training data and customers now average 9.0 hours, usage has shifted by 25%, beyond a 15% tolerance: investigate, and consider retraining.

quickCheck.explanation: A good test score is an estimate for the data it came from. Reliability means documenting what the model assumes and watching for changes in the data or outcomes after launch. Retuning on the test set would ruin its value as a final check.
options: Document the assumptions and limits, deploy it, and keep monitoring outcomes and incoming data so drift is noticed and the model can be retrained
Retune the settings on the test set to squeeze out a higher score before launch
Deploy it and stop, because the test score proves the model will stay accurate
Discard the validation results, because only the test score matters
quickCheck.question: The final model has been locked and scores well on the test set. Which next step best reflects a reliable ML workflow?

theory.body: A reliable ML project is a disciplined, iterative process, not "pick an algorithm, train, done". For churn: frame the problem; define features and target; check for leakage; split the data; establish a baseline; choose candidate models; train; evaluate on validation data; diagnose underfitting and overfitting; tune hyperparameters; compare candidates; lock the model and its settings; evaluate once on the test set; document assumptions and limits; monitor after deployment.
theory.heading: The whole loop

theory.body: With the model locked (tree-style, maximum depth 4), the 150 test customers, of whom 28 churn, give 22 true positives, 19 false positives, 6 false negatives and 103 true negatives. Precision is 0.54, recall 0.79 and F1 0.64, against validation F1 0.68. A small drop is normal: validation was used to make choices, the test set was not.
theory.heading: Evaluate once on the test set

theory.body: Recall 0.79 is at least 0.75 and precision 0.54 is at least 0.50, so the goal is still met, with less margin than validation suggested. Write down what the model was trained on, how it was evaluated, what it is for and its limits: it is trained on past customers, scored on a first-of-month snapshot and tuned for recall.
theory.heading: Check against the goal, then document

theory.body: A good test score is necessary but does not prove the model will stay good. The world changes: a new pricing plan, a competitor or a seasonal pattern can shift the customers' behaviour. This is data drift. A model trained on last year's customers can quietly become less accurate when conditions change.
theory.heading: Performance is not reliability

theory.body: After deployment, keep checking. Track the model's recall and precision as outcomes become known, and compare incoming feature values with the training data, such as the average monthly usage. A large shift is a signal to investigate and possibly retrain with new data. How large a shift matters depends on the problem, so the tolerance in our example is only a teaching value. The loop does not end at launch.
theory.heading: Monitor and iterate
